outgoing.name: Africa
outgoing.excerpt: It is a tropical tree, native to eastern Africa, including parts of the Madagascar dry deciduous forests.

outgoing.name: Arabic language
outgoing.excerpt: Alternative names include Indian date, translation of Arabic تمر هندي tamr hindī.

outgoing.name: Asia
outgoing.excerpt: It grows wild throughout the Sudan but has now been introduced into most of tropical Asia as well as Latin America and the Caribbean.

outgoing.name: Fruit
outgoing.excerpt: The fruit is a brown pod-like legume, which contains a soft pulp and many hard-coated seeds.

outgoing.name: Indonesian language
outgoing.excerpt: In Indonesia it is called asem (or asam) Jawa (means Javanese asam) in Indonesian.

outgoing.name: Latin America
outgoing.excerpt: It grows wild throughout the Sudan but has now been introduced into most of tropical Asia as well as Latin America and the Caribbean.

outgoing.name: Malaysia
outgoing.excerpt: In Malaysia it is called asam in Malay and swee boey in Hokkien.

outgoing.name: Philippines
outgoing.excerpt: For example, in the Philippines, the leaves have been traditionally used in herbal tea for reducing malaria fever.

outgoing.name: Sudan
outgoing.excerpt: It grows wild throughout the Sudan but has now been introduced into most of tropical Asia as well as Latin America and the Caribbean.

outgoing.name: Tamil language
outgoing.excerpt: In Sinhala the name is siyambala, in Telugu it is called Chintachettu (tree) and Chintapandu (fruit extract) and in Tamil and Malayalam it is puli.
